q: Five kids read 10, 20, 20, 30 and 120 minutes. Which is bigger, the mean or the median?
why: The median is 20, the middle number. The mean is 200 ÷ 5 = 40. The 120 is an outlier that pulls the mean up toward it.

q: Ana's test score has a z-score of −1.5. What does that mean?
choices: She scored 1.5 standard deviations below the mean
why: A z-score counts standard deviations, not points. Negative means below the mean.

q: A histogram has a long tail stretching to the right. What shape is it?
why: Skew is named after the tail. Tail on the right means skewed right, like incomes, where a few people earn a lot.

q: Which is a good investigative question for a statistical study?
choices: What is the typical height of 10th graders at our school?
How many inches are in 5 feet?
why: An investigative question is about a group and needs data that varies from person to person. Maya's height is just one number, and the others can't be answered with data.

q: A radio show asks listeners to call in and vote. What's the problem?
why: Only people with strong feelings bother to call, so their answers don't match everyone's.

q: Researchers want to show that a new app CAUSES better grades. What do they need?
why: Only a randomized experiment can show cause and effect. Random assignment makes the groups fair, so the app is the main difference.

q: A school splits students by grade (9, 10, 11, 12) and randomly picks 25 from each grade. What kind of sample is this?
why: Splitting into similar groups and sampling from EACH one is stratified. A cluster sample would pick a few whole groups.

q: Which one is a parameter?
choices: The mean of your sample of 40 students
The true percent of ALL U.S. teens who own a phone
why: A parameter describes the whole population. The others all come from a sample, so they're statistics.

q: 12 of 20 ninth graders and 6 of 15 tenth graders play a sport. What's the best way to compare the two grades?
why: The groups are different sizes, so compare percents: 12 ÷ 20 = 60% and 6 ÷ 15 = 40%.

q: You flip a fair coin 3 times. What's the probability of 3 heads?
why: Flips are independent, so multiply: ½ × ½ × ½ = 1/8.

q: A computer flips 5 coins, 1,000 separate times. In 498 of the tries there were at least 3 heads. What's the estimated probability of at least 3 heads?
why: A simulation estimates a probability with the fraction of tries where it happened: 498 ÷ 1,000 = 0.498. (The exact answer is 0.5, so the estimate is close.)

q: A game costs $1 to play. You win $5 with probability 0.1, and otherwise nothing. What's your expected profit per game?
why: Expected winnings = 5 × 0.1 = $0.50. Take away the $1 cost: 0.50 − 1 = −$0.50. On average you lose 50 cents a game.

q: A basketball player makes 70% of her free throws. You count how many she makes in 10 shots. Which distribution fits?
why: A set number of tries (10), each one make-or-miss with the same 70% chance, and the shots are independent. That's binomial.

q: P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.5, and A and B are independent. What is P(A and B)?
why: For independent events, multiply: 0.3 × 0.5 = 0.15.

q: Heights are normal with mean 64 inches and SD 3 inches. About what percent are between 61 and 67 inches?
why: 61 and 67 are each 1 SD from the mean (64 ± 3). The 68–95–99.7 rule says about 68% are within 1 SD.

q: Wait times are strongly skewed right. You take many samples of n = 50 and graph the sample means. What shape do you get?
why: The central limit theorem: with n ≥ 30, sample means make a bell shape even if the population is skewed.

q: A 95% confidence interval for the percent of students who like the new lunch is 0.48 to 0.58. What's the best interpretation?
choices: There's a 95% chance the true percent is 0.53
We are 95% confident the interval from 48% to 58% captures the true percent of all students who like the new lunch
why: Talk about capturing the true value, name the population, and use context. That's the AP template.

q: A test gives a p-value of 0.003 with α = 0.05. What should you do?
choices: Reject H₀: there's convincing evidence for Hₐ
Say you proved Hₐ is true
why: 0.003 is less than 0.05, so results like these would be very rare by luck alone. Reject H₀. We never “prove” Hₐ or “accept” H₀.

q: H₀ says a new medicine does nothing. Which is a Type I error?
choices: Saying it works when it really does nothing
Saying it does nothing when it really works
why: A Type I error is a false alarm: rejecting H₀ when H₀ is actually true.

q: Which change makes a significance test more powerful (better at catching a real effect)?
choices: A smaller α, like 0.01 instead of 0.05
why: More data makes a real effect easier to spot, so power goes up. A smaller α makes it harder to reject H₀, so power goes down.

q: How can you make a confidence interval narrower?
why: A bigger n shrinks the standard error, so the margin of error gets smaller. A higher confidence level makes the interval wider.

q: A random sample of students gives each one's grade (9 to 12) and favorite lunch (pizza, tacos or salad). Which test checks whether grade and favorite lunch are linked?
why: Two category variables from one sample, counted in a two-way table: that's a chi-square test for independence.

q: A two-way table has 4 rows and 3 columns. What are the degrees of freedom for a chi-square test?
why: df = (rows − 1)(columns − 1) = 3 × 2 = 6.

q: The sample size goes from 25 to 100. What happens to the spread of the sampling distribution of x̄?
why: The SD of x̄ is σ/√n. √100 = 10 and √25 = 5, so the spread is half as big. Four times the sample, half the wobble.

q: Why do we use t instead of z for means?
choices: We don't know the population SD σ, so we use s from the sample
t only works for big samples
why: Using s instead of σ adds extra wobble. The t-distribution has fatter tails to allow for it.

q: The same 15 runners are timed before and after a training plan. Which test fits?
choices: Paired t-test for the mean difference
why: Each runner gives two linked numbers, so it's paired. Subtract to get 15 differences and run a one-sample t-test on their mean.

q: A regression line is ŷ = 50 + 5x, where x is hours studied and ŷ is the predicted test score. What does the 5 mean?
choices: For each extra hour studied, the predicted score goes up 5 points
The predicted score is 5 when hours = 0
why: The slope is the change in predicted y for each 1 more x. Always say “predicted” and use the story's words.

q: For kids in grades 1 to 6, shoe size and reading level have r = 0.8. What's the best explanation?
choices: Big feet make you read better
Age is a confounding variable: older kids have bigger feet and read better
The correlation must be a mistake
why: Correlation isn't causation. Age is linked to both shoe size and reading level.

q: A point is at (4, 30). The line predicts ŷ = 35 when x = 4. What's the residual?
why: Residual = actual − predicted = 30 − 35 = −5. Negative means the point is below the line.

q: A residual plot shows a clear U-shaped curve. What does that tell you?
choices: A straight line is a good fit
A curved model would fit better than a straight line
why: Residuals should look like random scatter. A curved pattern means the line misses in a pattern, so the relationship is really curved.

q: A regression of test score on hours studied has r² = 0.64. What does that mean?
choices: About 64% of the variation in test scores is explained by the line using hours studied
why: r² is the percent of the change in y that the line explains. (Here r would be 0.8, not 0.64.)
